title: Playing Music on Axial-Flux Motors
summary: You're telling me my inverter can play AC/DC?
body_markdown:
Figure 1. The MC0-500 playing Back in Black through an axial-flux motor.


A common demonstration done by many makers online is to play music out of a motor (e.g., drone motor, stepper motor, brushed DC motor). In fact, certain varieties of drone ESC will purposefully play music out of the motor on startup (e.g., Bluejay / BLHeli). However, most of these demos use small motors with small motor controllers. Most discourse around making sound using large motors amounts to car enthusiasts complaining about the relative silence of EV powertrains.


Although it is rare to see, it's possible to do the same type of demo using a much larger motor.


## How does the motor make sound?


The rotor in a motor experiences forces axially, radially, and tangentially. Generally, when modelling a motor, we only care about the forces that are tangential to the rotor (i.e., forces that produce torque). Many motor models (e.g., those in\[1\] ) reflect this focus, as they elide the axial and radial forces. However, these forces contribute significantly to sound.


While both radial and axial flux motors can make sound, the disk-shaped rotor in an axial flux motor tends to produce more noise when it vibrates.


Figure 2. Radial-flux vs. axial-flux motor.

Therefore, for the purpose of vibrating the rotor to play specific audio (i.e., up to ~15.6 kHz, well above ω\\omega


for our purposes), it is sufficient to modulate vdv_d


at similarly high frequencies.


## Actually playing music


The Steinmetz MC0-500 is a high performance, high power traction inverter. Its high switching frequency allows us to modulate vdv_d


at 31.25 kHz. Additionally, its support for 100BASE-T1 automotive ethernet allows us to easily livestream uncompressed S16LE audio (a 500 kbps bit rate) into the firmware.


These two aspects mean that we truly use the inverter as a networked speaker, as opposed to using it as a MIDI-style device to play sine waves hardcoded into the firmware.
